items.title: OpenAI ships 12-hour prompt caching in the API
items.summary: You can now choose 12-hour prompt caching for shared instructions, tools and context, so requests hours apart still hit a warm cache instead of paying full input price. 12-hour cache writes cost 2.5x the input token price.
items.why: Longer-lived agent sessions and daily-cron-style workflows that only touch the API every few hours can now keep their system-prompt/tool-schema cache warm instead of re-paying full price every call.
items.action: If you have an agent or workflow that calls the API in bursts hours apart, switch its cache TTL to 12h and compare cached-vs-uncached cost on your next run.

eval.reason: Genuine new API capability extending cache retention; not a duplicate of any prior day's items.

items.title: Recursive ships Flint-40B-A2B, a fast local coding model built by its own automated research system
items.summary: Recursive's first model release: a 40B-parameter, 2.5B-active local coding model, built using Recursive's automated research system. Recursive's own reported benchmark and speed figures are circulating alongside the release (not independently verified here); the model is already listed in Ollama's library and drawing third-party test coverage.
items.why: A usably fast, open, local coding model is the kind of thing that actually changes a daily workflow if the numbers hold up — worth watching for independent verification before leaning on the vendor's own figures.
items.action: If you run local coding models, pull it via Ollama and run your own quick eval before trusting Recursive's reported benchmark numbers.

items.title: Serkan Ozal: the first "honest" raw LLM code-review benchmark — 7,980 reviews, no framework scaffolding
items.summary: 21 models across up to 3 reasoning-effort levels, 3 passes each, 7,980 reviews total on 50 real PRs across 5 projects, judged by Martian's Code Review Bench. Claude Sonnet 5.5 at low effort scores highest (F2 64.4) at $0.142/PR and a 9-second median; Muse Spark 1.3 at low effort is the best value in the top group at $0.062/PR. Code and data are open.
items.why: This is a rare raw, apples-to-apples look at which model and effort combination actually catches real bugs in real PRs per dollar, not a vendor-cherry-picked benchmark.
items.action: If you're picking a model for automated PR review, start from this cost/quality table instead of a generic leaderboard — low-effort Sonnet 5.5 or Muse Spark 1.3 look like the practical defaults.

items.title: Elvis Saravia shares "MemoryTax": when a memory layer actually beats full context, and when it doesn't
items.summary: Zedong Peng's paper finds Mem0-style memory only beats dumping the full context when the underlying model is weak (GPT-4o-mini); with a stronger model like Claude Opus 5.5, a simple raw-history-search agent (Pi) tops the cost-accuracy frontier at 99% accuracy for under half the cost of full-context.
items.why: A good argument against reaching for a memory framework by default — test raw context search against your actual model first, since the 'memory tax' often isn't worth paying.
items.action: Before adding a memory layer to an agent, benchmark plain full-context or raw-history search against it on your actual model — the paper suggests the fancier option frequently loses on cost-adjusted accuracy.

items.title: swyx: Opus 5.5 is the best work-estimator model he's used — and that calibration matters as more work gets delegated
items.summary: "Opus 5.5 is the best work estimator model i've ever used... don't tell me that it's going to take 2-3 working days (what a human would do) when for you... can get it done in 2-3 hours." Framed as a reason agent task-time estimates need their own calibration, not a human-timescale default.
items.why: As more day-to-day work gets delegated to agents, trusting a model's own honest time estimate instead of a human-scaled guess is becoming a real planning skill, not a nice-to-have.
items.action: Next time you scope a task for an agent, ask it to estimate its own completion time explicitly and compare that against your human-scale gut estimate before committing to a deadline.

items.title: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, its own production inference engine
items.summary: DeepSeek released DeepInfer (Apache-2.0, 19.4k stars already) — the actual high-performance, large-scale inference framework powering DeepSeek's production services, including DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, built on top of vLLM with speculative decoding and distributed-inference support across NVIDIA and Huawei hardware.
items.why: A frontier lab sharing its real production serving stack, not just model weights, is directly useful for anyone self-hosting open models and trying to close the throughput/cost gap with the big labs.
items.action: If you're self-hosting any DeepSeek model on vLLM today, worth a spin to compare DeepInfer's throughput and cost against your current setup.

items.title: Google Cloud Tech: "AI harness crash course" — what actually sits between the model and your files
items.summary: Annie Wang walks through four parts of an AI harness: context & memory, tools & execution flow, runtime/security/privacy, and evaluation — the software layer that lets a model open files, run tests, or ask before doing something risky, rather than the model itself.
items.why: A clear, first-party breakdown of harness architecture from the people building agent tooling at Google Cloud — useful framing for anyone building or evaluating a coding agent's harness, not just prompting it.
items.action: 9.5 minutes. Worth it if you want a clean mental model for 'harness vs. model' before your next harness design decision.

items.title: AI Engineer: "Better AI Models Won't Fix Your Engineering Team" — Jellyfish's 50,000-engineer dataset
items.summary: Nicholas Arcolano (Jellyfish) breaks down what actually drives AI-coding throughput across ~50,000 engineers at 447 companies: the tool itself explains under 1%, skill use ~3% (heavy skill users see ~30% more), token usage ~9%, company/team ~12%, and the individual engineer accounts for most of the rest — including a finding that pushing users from Cursor onto Grok barely moved merged PRs.
items.why: Hard data against the 'just give the team a better model' instinct — useful ammunition if you're making a case for investing in skills and process over model switching.
items.action: 16.5 minutes. The breakdown of what explains throughput variance is the part worth not skipping if you only watch one segment.

eval.reason: Data-driven talk (50,000 engineers, 447 companies) on what actually drives AI-coding throughput; genuinely new (posted Oct 23), not a rehash.
